name: CN XII Hypoglossal nerve
modality: Motor (somatic motor to all the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus); no sensory, no parasympathetic component
course: The preolivary sulcus of the medulla, between the pyramid and the inferior olive, gives rise to a linear series of 10–15 fine filaments at the landmark `surf-cn12-exit`; their short cisternal course — the rootlets run through the cerebellomedullary (lateral medullary) cistern, which is the segment a vertebral or PICA aneurysm can compress — converges laterally and anteriorly into two bundles that pierce the dura and pass through the hypoglossal canal of the occipital bone — the foramen this nerve uses — with a meningeal branch and the venous plexus, where the vertebral artery's course around the canal is the clinically load-bearing relationship (an aberrant or dolichoectatic vertebral artery, or a dissection, compresses the nerve inside the canal). Outside the skull the nerve descends between the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein, loops forward around the occipital artery and the sternocleidomastoid branch, crosses the internal and external carotid arteries and the lingual artery, and runs forward above the hyoid and deep to the mylohyoid and the posterior digastric to distribute to the tongue, carrying with it the C1 fibres that supply the geniohyoid and the thyrohyoid. Its long, looped course means it is injured in the neck as well as in the canal.
function: The motor nerve of the tongue: it innervates all the intrinsic muscles (which change the tongue's shape) and all the extrinsic muscles except palatoglossus — genioglossus (which protrudes the tongue), hyoglossus (which depresses it), styloglossus (which retracts and elevates it) and the rest — so it is the nerve of articulation, mastication, swallowing and airway protection. The genioglossus is the key muscle clinically: it pulls the tongue forward and is the muscle that keeps the airway open in sleep, which is why hypoglossal dysfunction causes obstructive sleep apnoea and why bilateral genioglossus paralysis obstructs the airway. Corticobulbar input to the hypoglossal nucleus is predominantly CONTRALATERAL for genioglossus, so a supranuclear lesion deviates the tongue away from the lesion, while a nuclear or nerve lesion deviates it TOWARD the lesion and adds wasting and fasciculations — the single most useful distinction this nerve offers at the bedside.

afferent: Hypoglossal nucleus (nuc-hypoglossal) — the somatic motor neurons, a paramedian column under the hypoglossal trigone of the fourth-ventricle floor; the rootlets leave the preolivary sulcus at `surf-cn12-exit`
Corticobulbar fibres from the motor cortex (ctx-m1) — predominantly contralateral for genioglossus, which is the anatomical reason a supranuclear lesion deviates the tongue away from the lesion

Reticular and solitary-nucleus inputs (nuc-solitarius-caudal, nuc-medullary-reticular) drive the tongue's automatic movements in swallowing and chewing, which is why the tongue can still swallow after a cortical lesion that has weakened voluntary protrusion
No sensory component: the tongue's sensation and taste travel with CN V (general sensation), CN VII, CN IX and CN X (taste)
efferent: Intrinsic muscles of the tongue (longitudinal, transverse and vertical) — shape and precision movements
Extrinsic muscles except palatoglossus: genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus and chondroglossus
The C1 fibres that travel with the nerve to the geniohyoid and thyrohyoid after leaving it in the neck — the anatomical reason this nerve is not purely 'cranial'

The nerve traverses the hypoglossal canal with the vertebral artery looping around the canal's outside (vasc-vertebral-artery), which is why an aberrant vertebral artery or a dissection produces an isolated twelfth-nerve palsy

bloodSupply: The cisternal rootlets and the canal segment are supplied by small branches of the vertebral artery (vasc-vertebral-artery) and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (vasc-posterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery); in the neck the nerve is supplied by the ascending pharyngeal and occipital arteries, whose branches it also crosses on its way to the tongue. The vertebral artery's relationship to the hypoglossal canal is the key vascular fact: the artery loops medially around the canal in most people, so a dolichoectatic or dissecting vertebral artery compresses the nerve against the canal's wall and produces an isolated hypoglossal palsy with tongue wasting — the classic vascular cause of a twelfth-nerve palsy, and the reason a hypoglossal palsy with neck pain or a headache must be investigated urgently for dissection.

clinical.syndrome: Hypoglossal (lower motor neuron) palsy — tongue deviates TOWARD the lesion
clinical.findings: The tongue is weak, wasted and fasciculating on the affected side and deviates TOWARD the side of the lesion on protrusion, because the intact contralateral genioglossus pushes the tip across the midline; speech becomes dysarthric (lingual consonants), chewing and swallowing are impaired, and in long-standing cases the tongue is visibly atrophic with a wrinkled mucosa. The side of the deviation therefore names the side of the lesion — the opposite of the supranuclear rule below.
clinical.vascular: Vertebral artery compression at the hypoglossal canal, or a medullary infarct (medial medullary syndrome); in the neck, carotid dissection, tumour or surgical injury
clinical.note: An isolated twelfth-nerve palsy demands imaging of the canal and the skull base: the nerve can be compressed by an aberrant vertebral artery, a meningioma, a chordoma or a metastasis at the occipital condyle.

clinical.syndrome: Supranuclear (corticobulbar) palsy — tongue deviates AWAY from the lesion
clinical.findings: A lesion above the nucleus (motor cortex, corona radiata, internal capsule) weakens the tongue contralaterally, and because genioglossus has predominantly contralateral cortical input the tongue deviates AWAY from the side of the hemispheric lesion; there is no wasting and no fasciculation, and the tongue retains its automatic movements in swallowing. A capsular lesion adds a contralateral hemiparesis, which is the localizing combination.
clinical.vascular: Middle cerebral artery territory or the internal capsule (vasc-middle-cerebral-artery; lenticulostriate perforators, vasc-lenticulostriate-arteries)
clinical.note: Tongue TOWARD the lesion = nuclear or nerve (lower motor neuron, with wasting); tongue AWAY = supranuclear. The presence of wasting and fasciculation settles it before any imaging.

clinical.syndrome: Medial medullary syndrome with hypoglossal involvement (Dejerine syndrome)
clinical.findings: An infarct of the medial medulla destroys the hypoglossal nerve's rootlets or nucleus together with the pyramid and the medial lemniscus: ipsilateral tongue weakness and wasting that deviates toward the lesion, contralateral hemiparesis, and contralateral loss of position and vibration sense — the three-way crossed pattern that names the level.
clinical.vascular: Anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery paramedian branches (vasc-vertebral-artery)
clinical.note: The hypoglossal palsy is the ipsilateral element; the crossed weakness and sensory loss are what separate a medullary lesion from an isolated nerve palsy.

clinical.syndrome: Bilateral hypoglossal palsy with tongue atrophy and obstructive sleep apnoea
clinical.findings: Bilateral involvement — motor neuron disease, syringobulbia, Chiari malformation, a foramen-magnum lesion or bilateral carotid dissection — produces a small, wrinkled, fasciculating tongue with severe dysarthria and dysphagia, and, because the genioglossus is the muscle that holds the airway open, obstructive sleep apnoea and respiratory failure in sleep; it is one of the bulbar presentations of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
clinical.note: The tongue is a muscle like any other, so bilateral lower-motor-neuron disease shows the full picture of atrophy, fasciculation and weakness — and the airway consequence is the immediate danger.
